comparison: Both address reporter mouse validation (C24-C27). OpenEval finds strong convergent evidence supporting successful generation, while peer reviewers express uncertainty about the 2A peptide design, fusion protein effects on MHC surface expression, and whether tomato release is required for fluorescence.

OpenEval R1 includes flow cytometry validation (C28-C31, C33-C35) that peer R2 addresses. OpenEval finds the data strongly supportive, while peer reviewers express uncertainty about magnitude differences between reporters and request methodological clarifications for flow cytometry experiments.

Both evaluate IFN-γ-induced reporter expression in vitro (C37-C38). OpenEval finds the data demonstrate expected responsiveness to inflammatory stimuli, while peer reviewers request higher magnification images, indicating uncertainty about image quality and sufficiency of evidence.

Both address baseline CNS expression patterns (C39-C45). OpenEval finds immunohistochemistry data well-characterize differential expression patterns consistent with known MHC biology, while peer reviewers express uncertainty requesting clarifications on cell identity, extent of expression in various regions, and better data organization.

Both evaluate EAE-induced MHC upregulation (C47-C52). OpenEval finds flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry data demonstrate expected patterns with appropriate statistics, while peer reviewers support the findings but request better image presentation and clarification of quantification methods.

Both address immune oligodendroglia quantification (C55-C62). OpenEval finds robust quantification with appropriate statistics supporting core findings, while peer reviewers express uncertainty noting borderline significance, high variability, need for clarification on lesion definition, and discrepancy with prior studies (0.6% vs 3-4%).

OpenEval R5 includes characterization of immune oligodendroglia as mature cells (C63-C65), while peer R7 addresses this finding. OpenEval finds PDGFRa and CC1 staining well-support the characterization, while peer reviewers express uncertainty requesting discussion of why OPC expression is much lower than CC1+ cells.

Both address lack of correlation between immune oligodendroglia and inflammation measures (C66-C67). OpenEval finds the negative result appropriately analyzed with reasonable inference about non-depletion, while peer reviewers express uncertainty requesting discussion of OPC vs mature oligodendrocyte differences, which relates to the interpretation of these findings.

Both evaluate astrocyte MHC upregulation (C68-C69). OpenEval finds clear immunohistochemical evidence supporting this secondary observation, while peer reviewers express uncertainty requesting more thorough discussion and interpretation of astrocyte reporter expression in inflammatory models.

OpenEval R8 addresses brain EAE findings (C70-C74), while peer R9 covers both brain EAE and AT-CUP model (C70-C80). OpenEval finds appropriate quantification and statistics with interesting differential correlations, while peer reviewers support the findings without major concerns, requesting only organizational improvements.

OpenEval R9 addresses AT-CUP model validation (C76-C80), covered in peer R9 alongside brain EAE data. OpenEval finds the regional analysis and inflammatory enrichment inference well-supported, while peer reviewers accept the demonstration that reporters work in multiple disease models.

Both evaluate scRNA-seq transcriptional validation (C81-C91). OpenEval finds appropriate sequencing depth and cell numbers with acknowledged limitations, while peer reviewers express significant uncertainty about multiple methodological concerns including n=1 experiment, tissue choice, viability bias, missing QC information, and TdT sequencing redundancy.

Both address oligodendroglial subpopulation characterization (C92-C105). OpenEval finds detailed transcriptional characterization with clear cluster definitions and appropriate contamination removal, while peer reviewers express uncertainty requesting further subclustering, additional markers, expanded discussion of MHC I cluster, and clearer presentation.

Both evaluate integration with published datasets (C106-C112). OpenEval finds reproducibility demonstrated with appropriate integration methods and reasonable explanations for differences, while peer reviewers support the analysis, noting it addressed their request for dataset integration despite methodological differences.

Both address major findings and conclusions (C113-C116, C125). OpenEval finds strong support from collective data with well-documented disease severity correlations and translational relevance, while peer reviewers support the overall conclusions, acknowledging the reporter lines as valuable tools despite requesting methodological improvements.

Both address speculative functional claims (C46, C100, C117-C119, C121-C124, C126-C128). OpenEval rates these as uncertain, noting they are biologically plausible hypotheses lacking direct experimental evidence, while peer reviewers support these forward-looking statements as appropriate speculation about utility and implications.

Both address literature-based background claims (C1-C23, C32, etc.). OpenEval finds these well-supported by cited literature providing appropriate context, while peer reviewers support these established findings, requesting only explanation of rationale for gene selection and discussion of MHC I expression patterns.

OpenEval R16 addresses future applications of reporter mice (C133-C134, C137-C138), finding these reasonable based on demonstrated utility. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these future application claims.

OpenEval R4 includes claims C53-C54 about statistical analyses supporting correlations with disease severity, which relate to peer R6's concerns about borderline significance and variability in the quantifications. OpenEval finds the statistics appropriate while peer reviewers note the results are borderline and variable.
